content.text:
I submitted **holistic** at 0.5 confidence. The data rule out part-based fairly well but don't cleanly separate holistic from factor-when-justified with k=3. I used the full budget of 60.

**Design:** I tracked one recombination target, `L1-S2-M3`. I trained tasks in three rounds so its three rules appeared in 1, then 2, then 3 trained tasks. Throughout, its highest similarity to any trained task stayed at 0.375 or below. Each test was compared with a control task whose rules were not reused.

**Results** (examples to criterion; lower means cheaper to learn; noise SD is about 15):

| Stage | Target `L1-S2-M3` | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Untrained | 39 (n=1) | 64 (n=1) |
| Each rule in 1 trained task | ~29 | `L4-S4-M4`: ~26 |
| Each rule in 2 trained tasks | ~40 (n=4) | not tested |
| Each rule in 3 trained tasks | 28 (n=16) | `L4-S4-M4`: 36 (n=10) |

- **Not part-based:** once every rule had been trained, the recombination should have been cheap, but it was no cheaper than the all-new task.
- **Not factor-when-justified with k=2:** at two appearances per rule the target showed no speedup.
- **k=3 is the open question:** at three appearances, both tasks had the same highest similarity to trained tasks (0.375). The target was somewhat cheaper (28 vs 36), but that gap is only about 1.5 standard errors. It's also smaller than I'd expect if all three rules had become reusable parts.
- **Similarity does matter:** `L3-S3-M2`, which matches a trained task on 75% of inputs, averaged about 20. That fits similarity-based transfer.

The main risk is that the learner is actually factor-when-justified with k=3 and the 28-vs-36 gap is real. That's why I put confidence at 0.5. More tests at the three-appearance stage would have been the way to settle it.
